title: In Glowsea, the attack you dodge can open the route you need
author: Training_Relation_89
selftext:
We publish Glowsea, an underwater stealth-and-rescue game built with AI assistance for code and artwork. Moving reveals your light; stopping dims it. A crab strike can break a barrier, so dodging can also open the route you need.

  
One practical lesson from the AI-assisted workflow: implementation checks and human play checks answer different questions. We are testing this by playing the real game with normal controls, rather than treating a successful build or a scripted route as proof that an encounter reads well. In one recent practice attempt, a failed encounter was followed by a successful attempt using shorter movement bursts. That second attempt still included observation pauses. It established that the objective was reachable; it did not establish that a new player could read and dodge the attacks smoothly. No difficulty change was made for the test.

  
That distinction also matters when interpreting feedback. A tester found that waiting out a watcher felt too safe. We kept that as a real pacing observation, passed it to the game owner, and left the exact encounter unknown. We have not turned it into a claimed reproducible defect or automatically increased enemy damage.

  
For the clip here, the narrower visual check is: can you see the barrier before the strike, the barrier breaking, and the route becoming usable? It contains edited normal-speed gameplay from two areas, including checkpoint continuation, with the original HUD and game audio. It is not a flawless continuous level clear.

  
For developers using AI to help implement encounters: what human play check has caught a problem that your implementation checks missed?

  
Publisher disclosure: this is our game. The complete first chapter is free in the browser, with no download or game account: [https://games.shapemo.com/play/glowsea/](https://games.shapemo.com/play/glowsea/)
